title: Mate in two: list every check, list every reply
outcomes: Lists every legal reply to a check: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king
Finds the mating move against each reply when a check starts a mate in two
Rejects a check that the defender can simply capture
Answers "no forced mate" when every check can be met

steps.text: A forced mate is found by **listing**, not by hoping. First write down every check. Then, for one check, list every reply: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king. The check starts a **mate in two** only if you have a mating move against *every* reply. If the list runs out, "no forced mate here" is a correct answer.

steps.caption: White to move. Qc8+ starts a mate in two. List Black's replies first.

line.say: Check along the diagonal. The king can step to h5, or the f-pawn can block.
The queen takes the blocker. Checkmate.

claims.statement: After Qc8+ the black king has one legal move.
After Qc8+ the f-pawn has one legal move, f5, which blocks the check.

steps.text: **Why the list matters.** A check can fail in three ways: the defender takes the checking piece, a block spoils your next move, or the king has a step you did not count. *Rule of thumb:* before you call a check a mate in two, try to take the checking piece with each enemy piece, king included. A check the king can simply capture is no threat at all.

steps.title: Same position, a different check
steps.prompt: In the first position Rb8+ forces mate in two. Now White tries the other check. Predict, then check.

steps.text: No labels now. Some of these positions have a mate in two and some do not. Run the same list: every check, every reply. The next three exercises are silent: no hints and no engine line until you answer.

steps.prompt: Think of the last silent exercise. Did you list the checks and the replies before you moved? In your own games, the next time you have a check, count the replies before you play it.
